faq.a: The fracture disrupts the quadriceps tendon attachment, reducing the lever arm needed for extension.
faq.q: Why does a patellar fracture impair knee extension?

faq.a: Immobilise the knee in extension, apply a cold pack, and arrange urgent imaging to rule out osteochondral injury.
faq.q: What is the first step in managing a lateral patellar dislocation?

faq.a: Yes; if the patella is high-riding (patella alta) on lateral view, suspect tendon rupture even if bone looks normal.
faq.q: Can a patellar tendon rupture be missed on X‑ray?

exam: A 19‑year‑old footballer presents with sudden anterior knee pain after a tackle – what is your immediate bedside assessment and why? — Check for swelling, patellar apprehension, quadriceps lag; these differentiate fracture, dislocation or tendinopathy.

Explain how the patella increases quadriceps efficiency – what would happen if the patella were absent? — It lengthens the lever arm; without it, knee extension force drops ~30 %, making walking difficult.

A patient with chronic malnutrition has a transverse patellar fracture – list the likely contributing factors and the most important investigation. — Osteopenia from vitamin D deficiency; obtain plain knee X‑ray to define fracture.

During a knee exam you note a positive grind test – what pathology does this suggest and what is the next step? — Likely chondromalacia patellae; advise activity modification and consider physiotherapy.

How would you differentiate a patellar tendon rupture from a quadriceps tendon rupture clinically? — Tendon rupture: high‑riding patella, inability to extend; quadriceps rupture: low‑riding patella, palpable gap above patella.

In a low‑resource clinic without radiography, a child presents with a swollen knee after a fall – how do you decide whether to refer for imaging? — Use criteria: inability to actively extend, visible deformity, open wound; if any present, arrange urgent referral.

What are the vascular risks of a displaced patellar fracture and how do you monitor them? — Injury to genicular arteries can cause haemarthrosis; monitor for expanding swelling and neurovascular status.
Why is NSAID use cautioned in a patient with active peptic ulcer disease who has patellar tendinopathy? — NSAIDs increase gastric bleeding risk; consider physiotherapy and topical agents instead.
ai.title: Patella Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The patella is the largest sesamoid bone, protecting the knee joint and enhancing quadriceps leverage. Understanding its relations, blood supply and common injuries is essential for low‑resource clinical practice.

b: Triangular shape, apex superior, base inferior
sections.p: The patella sits in the front of the knee joint, embedded in the quadriceps tendon and articulating with the femoral trochlea.

b: Anterior surface: shallow groove for quadriceps tendon
Posterior surface: articular cartilage covering trochlear groove
sections.p: It lies anterior to the distal femur, between the quadriceps tendon above and the patellar ligament below.

b: Vastus medialis obliquus (VMO) reinforces medial border
sections.p: Anteriorly covered by skin and subcutaneous tissue; deep to the quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament; laterally bounded by the vastus lateralis and medially by the vastus medialis.

b: Superior medial and lateral genicular arteries (proximal pole)
Inferior medial and lateral genicular arteries (distal pole)
sections.p: Supplied by a rich peripatellar anastomosis from the genicular arteries.

b: Femoral nerve – skin over anterior patella
sections.p: Sensory innervation from branches of the femoral nerve (anterior cutaneous branches) and the common peroneal nerve.

b: Protects the anterior knee joint from trauma
sections.p: Acts as a fulcrum to increase the moment arm of the quadriceps, improving knee extension strength.

b: Patellar fracture – usually from direct blow; look for swelling, inability to extend knee
Patellar dislocation – lateral displacement; assess for hemarthrosis and ligament injury
Patellar tendinopathy – anterior knee pain in athletes; worsens with jumping
sections.p: Patellar fractures, dislocations and tendinopathies are common, especially in active youths and in patients with malnutrition or chronic infections that weaken bone.

t.b: Confirms fracture pattern or dislocation; if unavailable, use clinical criteria (deformity, loss of extension) to decide on splinting
Detects tendon tears or fluid collections; useful where X‑ray is unavailable

b: Patellar apprehension test – positive if patient resists lateral displacement
Quadriceps lag – inability to actively extend knee despite intact reflexes
Patellar grind test – pain with compression and patellar movement indicates chondromalacia
sections.p: Key bedside findings help differentiate patellar pathology from other knee problems.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe swelling with loss of active knee extension
Open fracture or wound over the patella
Signs of vascular compromise (pale foot, absent pulses) after dislocation
